extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and instructors in differential equations and dynamical systems
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical methods for ordinary differential equations and dynamical systems: existence/uniqueness/regularity results, linearization and variational equations, continuous dependence on data and parameters, and basic numerical integrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steady-state solution for forced, damped harmonic oscillator
rubrics_metrics.description: For x'' + b x' + k x = cos t with k, b > 0, there exists a unique 2π-periodic steady-state solution and every solution tends to that steady-state as t → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The steady-state initial condition X0 is found by solving (exp(2πA) − I) X0 = −W; invertibility of exp(2πA) − I (see next criterion) guarantees uniqueness. Physically: damping causes transient homogeneous motion to decay, leaving only motion due to periodic forcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertibility criterion for exp(2πA) − I
rubrics_metrics.description: The matrix exp(2πA) − I is invertible provided exp(2πA) has no eigenvalue 1; equivalently, if all eigenvalues λj of A have Re(λj) < 0 then |exp(2πλj)| < 1 so exp(2πA) − I is invertible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show uniqueness of periodic initial value X0 for forced linear systems; anti-pattern: if exp(2πA) has eigenvalue 1, the corresponding periodic solution initial value is not uniquely solvable via this linear algebraic inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodicity vs quasiperiodicity for undamped forced oscillator
rubrics_metrics.description: For the undamped forced oscillator with forcing frequency ω, the general solution contains terms with periods 2π and 2π/ω; the solution is periodic if and only if ω is a rational number; if ω is irrational the motion is quasiperiodic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit solution formulas show first term period 2π, second period 2π/ω. Use rationality of frequency ratio to determine periodicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and Uniqueness Theorem (local)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X' = F(X) with F : R^n → R^n of class C1, for any initial condition X(t0)=X0 there exists a unique solution X defined on some interval (t0 − a, t0 + a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis: F is continuously differentiable (C1). Proof uses Picard iteration. Anti-patterns: discontinuous F can yield no solution (example given), nondifferentiable F can yield non-uniqueness (example x' = 3 x^{2/3}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard iteration as constructive existence method
rubrics_metrics.description: Define u0(t)=x0 and uk+1(t)=x0 + ∫_0^t F(uk(s)) ds; under the C1 hypothesis this sequence converges to the unique solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how the iteration produces familiar series (e.g., exponentials, sine/cosine). Use Picard iteration both as a proof technique and as an intuition for successive approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathologies when hypotheses fail
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is not continuous at a point, solutions may not exist through that point; if F is continuous but not differentiable, multiple solutions through the same initial condition may exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two canonical examples are provided: a discontinuous vector field on R with no solution through 0, and x' = 3 x^{2/3} which admits infinitely many solutions through 0. Use these as anti-pattern checks when checking hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal interval blow-up property
rubrics_metrics.description: If X(t) is a solution defined on maximal open interval J=(α,β) with β<∞ and U⊂R^n open, then for every closed bounded K⊂U there exists some t in (α,β) with X(t) ∉ K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: if a solution cannot be extended past β it must leave every compact subset of the domain (approach the boundary or blow up). Use this to diagnose finite-time blow-up or approach to domain boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous dependence on initial conditions (stability estimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is C1 and X(t) is a solution on [t0,t1] with X(t0)=X0, then there exists a neighborhood U of X0 and constant K such that for any Y0∈U the unique solution Y(t) with Y(t0)=Y0 is defined on [t0,t1] and satisfies |Y(t) − X(t)| ≤ |Y0 − X0| exp(K(t − t0)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the flow φ(t,X) is continuous in X. The bound gives explicit exponential separation control; use to show small initial perturbations remain small for finite time (at most exponential growth). Example provided demonstrating exponential separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous dependence on parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: If X' = F_a(X) depends on a parameter a and F_a is continuously differentiable in both X and a, then the flow depends continuously on the parameter a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: augment system with a' = 0 to convert parameter-dependence into initial-condition dependence and apply continuous dependence on initial data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness of flows (regularity of φ)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is C1 then the flow φ(t,X) of X' = F(X) is a C1 function in both t and X; in particular ∂φ/∂t and ∂φ/∂X exist and are continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: ∂φ/∂t(t,X0) = F(φ(t,X0)); ∂φ/∂X(t,X0)=Dφ_t(X0). This justifies differentiating flow w.r.t. initial conditions and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonautonomous linear system existence
rubrics_metrics.description: For X' = A(t) X with A(t) a continuous family of n×n matrices on [α,β], the initial value problem X(t0)=X0 has a unique solution defined for all t∈[α,β].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity of A(t) (not C1) suffices. Also: solutions obey the linearity principle (linear combinations of solutions are solutions). Example: scalar x' = a(t)x has solution x(t)=x0 exp(∫_0^t a(s) ds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variational equation / linearization along a solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a solution X(t) of X' = F(X), set A(t)=DF(X(t)). The variational equation U' = A(t) U is a linear nonautonomous system whose solution U(t) approximates the effect of small perturbations in initial conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition: if Y(t) is the solution with Y(t0)=X0+U0 and U(t) solves the variational equation with U(t0)=U0, then |Y(t) − (X(t)+U(t))| / |U0| → 0 uniformly as U0→0 on bounded time intervals. Also Dφ_t(X0) U0 = U(t,U0). Use U(t) (linear in U0) as practical first-order approximation to nearby nonlinear trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearization at equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: At an equilibrium X0 of X' = F(X), the Jacobian A = DF(X0) gives the linearized autonomous system U' = A U; near X0 the nonlinear flow resembles the flow of this linearized system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because DF(X0) is constant, the variational equation reduces to the autonomous linear system whose flow is exp(tA). Use this to classify local phase portrait types near equilibria (to be made precise in subsequent chapters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dφ computation via variational equation
rubrics_metrics.description: The derivative of the time-t map satisfies Dφ_t(X0) U0 = U(t,U0), where U(t,U0) is the solution of the variational equation U' = D F(X(t)) U with U(0)=U0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recipe: compute the Jacobian along the known solution X(t), solve the linear variational system for each basis U0 to obtain the Jacobian matrix Dφ_t(X0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical integrators: Euler, Improved Euler, Runge–Kutta (order-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three iterative one-step methods for approximating solutions x' = f(t,x): Euler: x_{k+1}=x_k + f(t_k,x_k) Δt. Improved Euler (Heun): x_{k+1}=x_k + (Δt/2)(m_k + n_k) where m_k=f(t_k,x_k), n_k=f(t_k+Δt, x_k + m_k Δt). Runge–Kutta 4th order: x_{k+1}=x_k + (Δt)(m_k + 2 n_k + 2 p_k + q_k)/6 with specified intermediate slopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All methods use fixed step tk+1 = tk + Δt; smaller Δt typically improves accuracy. RK4 is the standard general-purpose solver; Heun reduces local error by averaging endpoint/initial slopes; Euler is simplest but least accurate/stable. Use appropriate step sizes and method depending on desired accuracy and stiffness.
